source_title: China ups the ante in Arunachal - India Today
source_excerpt: The flashpoints in Ladakh along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) between India and China have been quiet for some time. The disquiet is now coming from Arunachal Pradesh, which has emerged as the focal point of border tensions. On October 22, speaking at the Indo-Tibetan Border Police’s (ITBP) Central Training College in Alwar, Director General Shatrujeet Kapur revealed face-offs with Chinese troops at multiple locations along the Arunachal border in recent days. Without naming specific areas, he also praised the force’s Shaurya commandos for performing “exceptionally well” during the confrontations. The comments triggered widespread concern. It was the first official acknowledgment of confrontations between border patrols despite the chatter on social media channels since July.Kapur’s remarks confirmed the open secret that ITBP and People’s Liberation Army (PLA) troops were engaged in face-offs in Asaphila, near Taksing in Arunachal’s Upper Subansiri district. These were followed by a corps commander-level meeting between the two sides on September 6 at the Wacha-Damai border meeting point to address friction on the LAC. After the talks, the PLA, Indian army and the ITBP reportedly reduced troop numbers from over 1,000 each in August to around 200 each in the Taksing and Limeking areas.Beneath the unease in military circles over the clashes lies a deep strategic worry: the possibility that Beijing is intensifying grey-zone operations in the eastern Himalayas by testing Indian responses and pushing boundaries in tactics typical of ‘salami slicing’.Asked about the clashes, external affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said on October 23, “The situation in the India-China border areas gets disturbed...when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns.” A NEW FLASHPOINTRugged terrain, difficult logistics and stretches requiring greater preparedness present operational challenges for the Indian army in Arunachal. Experts believe China is willing to test the limits of existing border-management mechanisms by probing Indian positions here. The question for New Delhi is whether these face-offs are isolated incidents or part of a calculated move to keep India under pressure.A senior military official believes that China has decided to ratchet up pressure on the LAC to keep alive its claim on Arunachal Pradesh. Also, in August, India formally identified 27 places and geographical features in the state by their standard names on the official Indian map, followed by 28 features in Ladakh. Calling this “hype”, China is responding on the ground.Lt Gen. S.L. Narasimhan (retd), former commander of Dimapur-based III Corps which is responsible for most of Arunachal Pradesh, notes that Chinese troops have been moving in and out of these areas for years. “This time, I believe, they have sat over there,” he said. “We have to be careful about anything unusual that they do. Until we clear the issue by exchanging maps, such problems will recur.”Sources indicate that the PLA’s Border Defence Regiments—frontline units responsible for patrolling and defending frontiers—have grown markedly more aggressive in the Arunachal sector over the past few months.Locals have repeatedly flagged Chinese presence in remote areas in Arunachal. In late June 2026, the Nah Welfare Society, a community organisation representing tribal residents in Taksing, submitted a formal memorandum to the district deputy commissioner of Upper Subansiri. It expressed “deep grief” over what it described as the occupation of ancestral lands by the PLA and claimed that the Chinese had constructed roads, bridges, camps and other infrastructure in areas considered Indian territory. The letter named five locations: Oying (Asaphila area), Paniar (Chujarta area), Marpan (Marnafe), Potrang Lake and Tindingtang.Speaking to india today over the phone, one resident alleges that the PLA crossed the LAC at Shera 4 and 5 (patrolling points in the Taksing sector), took control of the Portang Lake.In August, a fact-finding team from the People’s Party of Arunachal Pradesh (PPA) also alleged that the PLA had denied the Indian Army access to key patrolling points in Taksing.Lt Gen. Rakesh Sharma (retd), former commander of the Leh-based 14 Corps, notes that since the Galwan clash in eastern ladakh in June 2020, India has a principle: Chinese troops must not be allowed to establish a presence in areas claimed by India. This has raised the risk of scuffles. “From Ladakh to Arunachal, we have decided to deploy our men in forward areas to prevent a Galwan-type situation,” he says.“India must adapt its border defence strategy to the realities of modern warfare, where drones, electronic warfare and real-time intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance systems are as critical as troop deployments and physical infrastructure,” says Lt Gen. Anil Ahuja (retd), who commanded a mountain division in Arunachal. He feels the army and the ITBP need a more integrated command, enabling them to share intelligence and respond swiftly to emerging threats. WHY ARUNACHAL MATTERSThough till the 1980s China laid claim to only Tawang, the broader claim to the entire state of Arunachal Pradesh—calling it South Tibet or Zangnan—was amplified only after that and more concertedly since the 2000s. Of the 3,488 km-long LAC, the longest stretch—over 1,080 km—lies along Arunachal Pradesh which, together with Sikkim, forms the eastern sector of the border with China.Among the three army corps responsible for this sector, 33 Corps in Sikkim is assessed as the strongest, while IV Corps (Gajraj Corps) covering the Tezpur–Tawang sector is also considered well-equipped. The III Corps, responsible for 80 per cent of Arunachal, is the weakest in terms of mobility.Lt Gen. Narasimhan explains that frontier areas such as Longju, Asaphila and Taksing have posed problems because of poor road connectivity. “Successive corps commanders, including myself, have tried to build roads up to the border, but the treacherous conditions make it extremely difficult. Until we achieve better connectivity, the only way to deal with such scenarios is increased surveillance using the latest technology.”A top military official points out that India is overly dependent on its air assets for logistics and deployment in many remote areas. In some sectors, Indian positions remain up to 80 km short of the LAC, leaving large stretches unmanned, and monitored only through long-range patrols. “Unlike Ladakh, the area was never prioritised by the Centre; the northern sector received preference for defence preparedness,” he says. INFRASTRUCTURE PUSHLt Gen. Rajeev Chaudhary (retd.), former Director General of the Border Roads Organisation (BRO), says China had benefitted from the relatively level terrain of the Tibetan plateau, while India’s roads had to be built along steep mountain slopes and through fragile terrain. “China has been way ahead of us in border infrastructure purely because it is sitting on a plateau, while we are on the slope, so it has the geographical advantage,” he says. China continues to strengthen its highway network, he says, making India’s own construction drive an operational necessity. However, surveying remote areas, building roads through dense forests and stabilising mountain slopes can take years. Chaudhary estimates that a substantial portion of the work in Arunachal Pradesh remains unfinished.The government has, nevertheless, accelerated infrastructure construction in recent years. In December 2025, defence minister Rajnath Singh inaugurated 32 BRO infrastructure projects in Arunachal Pradesh, including roads, tunnels, bridges and a helipad-related initiative. Project Brahmank of the BRO maintains 811 km of roads and 86 bridges across the sensitive border districts of Siang, West Siang, Upper Siang and Shi-Yomi. Under the central Vibrant Villages Programme, the state has approved 1,022 km of strategic roads worth Rs 2,205 crore to provide last-mile connectivity for 126 critical border villages across 11 districts.India’s infrastructure drive is unfolding alongside China’s border settlements or villages under its Xiaokang programme, with a substantial number of 628 villages facing Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh. With roads, telecommunications and infrastructure, they improve logistics, surveillance and mobility at the LAC for China.Militarily, China’s approach combines forward border defence units, with larger Combined Arms Brigades (CABs)—integrating infantry with armour, artillery, air defence, logistics and electronic warfare—for greater support. Its road rail and air infrastructure across Tibet can facilitate swift mobilisation too.India, meanwhile, benefits from long-established military deployments, local terrain knowledge, airlift capabilities and a fast expanding road network. Its priorities are to improve forward access and strengthen supply lines, expand surveillance, ensure reliable communications and thus increase its capacity to respond to local incidents quickly and effectively.UNITED AGAINST THE SIANG PROJECTA kind for kind strategic reply to China’s mammoth upstream dam in Tibet runs into local resistance A roadblock by anti-dam protestersIndia’s proposed 11,200 MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) in Arunachal Pradesh is caught in a tangle of local opposition. Conceived as a hydropower and infrastructure initiative, it is claimed that the project on the Siang river will help manage water-related risks by being a strategic buffer to China’s Medog dam project further upstream. The agitation centres on drilling and other work for the project’s pre-feasibility study without the consent of local communities. Many fear that it would lead to displacement, widespread environmental damage and loss of ancestral lands.The Siang river originates in Tibet as the Yarlung Tsangpo, before it enters Arunachal and then flows into Assam as the Brahmaputra. In July 2025, China began constructing a massive, 60,000 MW hydropower project near the Tsangpo’s ‘great bend’ in Tibet. The project has heightened Indian concerns about downstream water security and floods. In August 2026, India urged China to resume sharing Tsangpo water-flow data and provide information about upstream infrastructure. For India, limited Chinese transparency has made the disruption of Siang-Brahmaputra’s water flow a possibility.Officials claim that the Siang dam’s storage and flow-regulation capabilities would help moderate flood events. Associated infrastructure would improve connectivity and create employment too.Experts say that independent environmental assessments, fair compensation and rehabilitation plans are essential, particularly in a seismically active region. Geeta Kochhar, senior assistant professor at JNU’s Centre for Chinese Studies, says, “As China expands its upstream dams, a large reservoir could help India manage sudden changes in river flows,” while adding that the concerns are legitimate and require credible safeguards.- Ends
